source.title: Is Exchangeability better than I.I.D to handle Data Distribution Shifts while Pooling Data for Data-scarce Medical image segmentation?
source.authors: Ayush Roy; Samin Enam; Jun Xia; V. Lokhande; Won Hwa Kim

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adding training samples changes test performance, using medical image segmentation and data-addition experiments rather than the original double-descent method. It does not locate an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own data-addition results relevant to V3. It does not sweep model size or epochs, or identify an interpolation threshold. The KL/JS divergence results describe dataset distribution differences, not test error. Results cited from other work are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study tests the 'data addition dilemma' (Shen et al., 2024): test accuracy drops when samples from a shifted source dataset are added. It cites Nakkiran et al. only in passing, about memorization and interpolation. It does not sweep model size, epochs or i.i.d. sample count, and does not locate an interpolation threshold. The authors attribute the harm to distributional divergence, not to the capacity-sample interplay V3 names. This is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that pooling or adding data from shifted sources degrades baseline segmentation performance, and that their exchangeability-based feature-discrepancy loss mitigates this. They explain the non-monotonic baseline trends in Fig. 3 by the KL/JS divergence at each addition step. They do not frame the effect as double descent or relate it to an interpolation threshold.
record.recipe_differences: Tests data addition in medical image segmentation under distribution shift, using segmentation losses and test-set performance; does not reproduce the original double-descent sweeps or interpolation-threshold analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported data-addition outcome depends on the loss used: naive, Lcon and Ldeeps decrease in test performance, whereas Lfd + Lexchfd is reported to improve overall performance. The data-addition settings also differ by dataset pair and addition schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding samples from a distribution-shifted source dataset lowers test performance on the base dataset for the naive, Ldeeps and Lcon baselines. The trend is non-monotonic and tracks KL/JS divergence between the base set and the added subset. Adding similar-distribution data (S2) improves performance, per Fig. 1b.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data addition dilemma: adding training data from a shifted source can raise test error on the original distribution, in proportion to the distributional divergence.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at MIDL 2026 (PMLR), as stated in the text.
record.problems: The paper does not identify an interpolation threshold, and the data-addition section provides no numeric per-step test-performance values in the text. The architecture and uncertainty for the data-addition results are not stated. The reported 7–19% Lcon drop is not allocated to individual setups or addition steps.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Distribution-divergence metrics in Tables 2–3 are not test-performance outcomes; other segmentation and Gaussian input-noise experiments do not test the listed double-descent versions.

untested.parts: No test error reported over epochs.
No i.i.d. sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold. The data-addition experiments concern cross-source distribution shift.
No label-noise or regularization sweep tied to a test-error peak. The Gaussian input-noise robustness test is unrelated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V3 'supports' label are rejected. V3's 'more data hurts' is specific to the interpolation threshold under the same distribution. Here the harm comes from cross-dataset shift, and the authors say same-distribution data helps. No version verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the size that just fits the training set.
The experiments do not establish whether additions occur near an interpolation threshold; they test additions under distribution shift, not the general sample-size curve.
Capacity-risk curves across model classes and interpolation points.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.

Whether label noise or variance drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them. The separate Gaussian input-noise robustness experiment does not test these claims.
Whether recounting complexity as effective parameters turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: model used in the TNBC–MoNuSeg data-addition experiment (architecture not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Sequentially add MoNuSeg samples to TNBC and evaluate on TNBC.
rows.value: Decreases as more samples from Dnovel are incorporated; numeric values not stated.
rows.note: The text explicitly reports this trend for the naive method. The additions are under distribution shift; proximity to an interpolation threshold is not reported.
rows.check: Measures harm from adding shifted-source (MoNuSeg) data, not sample-wise double descent near an interpolation threshold. The text also calls the Fig. 3 trends non-monotonic (dip, peak, dip), tied to KL/JS divergence, not a simple decrease.

rows.subject: model used in the US-TNBC–UDIAT data-addition experiment (architecture not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Add UDIAT samples in batches of 15 to US-TNBC and evaluate on US-TNBC.
rows.value: Decreases as more samples from Dnovel are incorporated; numeric values not stated.
rows.note: The text explicitly reports this trend for the naive method. The additions are under distribution shift; proximity to an interpolation threshold is not reported.
rows.check: Distribution-shift data addition (UDIAT into US-TNBC), not V3. Authors describe the baselines peaking at later steps as divergence falls, so 'decreases' oversimplifies the trend.
